Stanford Company Board

Use the accelerator buttons first — the whole list is deliberately long, and the filters are how you cut it to something readable.

Three observations

The three layers are almost completely disjoint. Only 15 companies carry both YC and StartX, out of 252 and 1266. Of the 28 hand-verified companies, 7 are in YC and exactly one is in StartX. A census built on any single source will therefore always look small, and that is the whole reason this board has three.

The biggest Stanford student companies went through no accelerator at all. Flapping Airplanes ($5.00B), Humans& ($4.48B), Simile ($2.00B), Axiom Math ($1.60B), Engram ($0.60B), Pika ($0.47B) and Cartesia appear in neither the YC nor the StartX directory. They raised directly from Sequoia, Index, GV, Greenoaks, NVIDIA, Lightspeed and General Catalyst. An accelerator is how a Stanford student with no track record gets a first cheque; it is visibly not how a Stanford PhD with a named research result gets one. CORRECTION WORTH RECORDING: an earlier draft of this board claimed StartX contained Humans&, Flapping Airplanes, Pika and Numbers Station. It did not. Those were false matches created by deduplicating on website domain when the hand-verified layer's link field holds the source article, so six companies collided on techcrunch.com. Press-link domains and shared event domains are now refused as match keys.

StartX's own headline figures, from its community page: over 3,000 Stanford-affiliated founders, $200B+ in total valuation, 29 unicorns and 144 startups valued above $100M. Note those disagree with third-party trackers, which variously report 20 unicorns, 5 unicorns and a $120B total. The spread is the finding: nobody agrees, and StartX is marking its own homework.

Degree level is knowable for roughly a third of the board and no more. 268 of 1522. That is a hard ceiling set by what founders choose to write about themselves, not something more searching would fix.

Where these companies came from

Ordered roughly by how low the barrier is. The first has no selection at all — admission is guaranteed to any Stanford student who fills in the form — and it exists specifically to help you find co-founders.

Stanford Venture Studio

Any Stanford-affiliated student

Admission is non-competitive — guaranteed to any Stanford student who submits the application form. 24/7 coworking, compute credits, mentoring, and mixers explicitly for founding-team formation. Recently expanded with dedicated AI labs giving student teams compute.

StartX

Stanford students, faculty and alumni

Zero equity, no fees. Reported $120B total portfolio valuation, average $42M raised per company; ~123 startups supported as of May 2026 with 5 unicorns and 32 exits; wider community 1,300 companies and 20 unicorns.

Cardinal Ventures

Stanford student teams

10-week program run twice a year (fall and spring), 12-20 teams admitted, weekly speaker sessions and structured workshops.

NFX FAST for Stanford

Stanford founders

Either a $150K discovery check on an uncapped SAFE, or a $1.5M-$3M pre-seed/seed for 15%. Application deadline 12 April. NFX partners Pete Flint, Anna Piñol and Valerie Osband Mahoney are Stanford alumni. NFX was first investor in Mammoth Biosciences, Arc, Jupiter, SESO — all Stanford.

Pear Garage / Pear Dorm

Engineering students at Stanford and Berkeley

Pear VC runs Garage for Bay Area engineering students and Dorm for student builders; winning teams get a $100K uncapped SAFE and a fast-track PearX partner meeting. Pear was the seed investor in Valar Labs (PearX S21).

Neo Scholars and Neo Residency

Students showing early technical promise

Neo Scholars: ~30 students a year, $20K grant plus mentor network — every one of OpenAI's new-grad hires in a recent year was a Neo scholar. Neo Residency: 5-8 students get $40K no-strings to take a semester off. Neo backed Cursor and Applied Compute.

Y Combinator Early Decision

Students who want to finish their degree

Launched Sept 2025: apply now, get funded the moment you are accepted, then do YC after graduation. In W26 Stanford had 22 founders in the batch (Berkeley 30, Harvard 18).

Z Fellows

Technical builders of any age, including students

One-week intensive, optional $10K investment at a $1B valuation cap. Many Stanford and MIT students participate while still enrolled.

a16z Speedrun

Any founder, heavily young-founder weighted

Up to $1M plus $10M+ in credits, 12 weeks in San Francisco. Acceptance rate below 0.4%. Over $180M deployed to 150+ startups.

Thiel Fellowship

Under-23s willing to leave school

$250,000 over two years in the 2026 class (up from $200K in 2025 and $100K before). 2026 cohort: 12 founders from 7 countries, including a Stanford CS student who was an MTS at OpenAI on agent memory and a Stanford AI Lab researcher. Prior fellows founded Anthropic, Cognition, Etched, Figma, Mercor.

Breakthrough Ventures

College students and recent grads

Student-run. Up to $100K grants, Microsoft and NVIDIA compute, $50K follow-on, Demo Day at Stanford.

AI for Healthcare Bootcamp (Stanford ML Group)

Stanford students

Its alumni started Valar Labs (a16z, $26M) and Wispr AI ($2B). This is the single highest-yield student program found in this pass relative to its size.

TreeHacks

Anyone, Stanford-hosted

12th annual edition in Feb 2026 awarded $500,000 in prizes, up from $200,000 in 2025. Sponsored by OpenAI, Google and Anthropic.

Stanford Horizons

Robotics and drone builders

Stanford robotics drone hackathon — the hardware-side counterpart to TreeHacks.

DAF-Stanford AI Studio

Students interested in defense AI

Department of the Air Force and Stanford joint studio. Context: Stanford's first defense-tech career fair drew 300 students, Stanford DEFCON drew 1,000+ attendees, and Stanford Women in National Security has 150+ members.

BASES

Undergrads, entry via Frosh Battalion in early fall

Runs the $100K pitch competition; you can apply to help run programs at the end of the school year.

ASES

Stanford students, founded 1989

12-week design-thinking bootcamp for freshmen culminating in a pitch to Silicon Valley investors.

Stanford Biotechnology Group / Students in Biodesign / SPARK

Bio-side students

The bio equivalents of the CS entry points; SPARK runs the translational-medicine startup pipeline.

Three layers, and what each can and cannot see

A. The YC census (252). YC's Algolia index carries no founder data, but every company page embeds a JSON blob with founders[] including a self-written bio. All 3,014 pages from Winter 2022 on were fetched, zero failures, 5,830 founder records, 97.6% with a bio. A company qualifies when a founder's own bio names Stanford as a personal affiliation. Tie kinds are read only within 150 characters of the word Stanford and a nearest-university rule discards degrees belonging to another school. Collaboration phrasing — "scientists from Stanford" — is subtracted before the personal test, which removed one false positive outright.

B. StartX (1266). The Stanford-affiliated accelerator: zero equity, no fees. Its community directory is a Webflow CMS list, 25 per page, 53 pages, harvested in full — 1,270 companies from the first 2010 session to Spring 2026. It carries session, industry, description and website. It carries no founders and no valuations, which is the single biggest limit on this board: for a StartX-only company there is no honest way to state a degree level, so it is left unknown.

C. Hand-verified (28). The earlier press pass. Kept because it is the only layer with valuations and named backers, and because it holds large companies neither directory contains. It is media-selected and therefore biased toward big rounds.

Dedupe. By normalised company name and by website domain, so a company in two layers is one row with both accelerator tags rather than two near-duplicates. 15 companies carry both YC and StartX.

Precision. On the YC layer, a random sample of 14 was hand-read against full bios and all 14 were true positives at company level. Tie-kind precision is lower, which is why levels like "Researcher, degree unstated" and "Stanford, capacity unstated" exist as their own categories instead of being forced into a degree.

What is still missing. The YC snapshot starts at Winter 2022, so earlier Stanford YC companies are invisible to layer A — Vori is a confirmed case, caught only by layer C. StartX's directory is the accelerator's own membership list, so a Stanford company that never applied is absent from both directories and can only arrive through the press layer. Bios are self-written, so a Stanford founder who did not say so is uncountable. 13 YC companies sit in an ambiguous bucket in the data file awaiting a human read. And no valuation was invented: a blank means no named outlet reported one, not that the company is worth nothing.

Reproducing it

tools/yc/scrape.py → tools/yc/founders.py → tools/yc/stanford_filter.py for layer A; tools/startx/scrape.py for layer B; then tools/stanford/build_board.py to merge all three and render this page. Every YC row keeps the evidence window its judgement rests on, in tools/yc/stanford_yc.json, so any classification here can be argued with by pointing at the text.
